title: LS Eco Energy to Build $8.5M Samarium Facility in Vietnam With Australia's Lynas
content:
Korea Supply Chain Brief · September 30, 2026

LS Eco Energy will invest KRW 11.6 billion (about $8.5 million) to build a samarium metal production facility in Vietnam, sourcing rare earth material from Australia's Lynas and supplying the metal to LS Cable & System's permanent magnet plant. Here is why samarium matters for defense and aerospace magnets, and how this fits into a rare-earth supply chain that currently runs almost entirely through China.

CompanyRoleEvidence
LS Eco Energy
KRX: 229640		Building the samarium metal production facility in VietnamAnnounced (company release, Sep 30, 2026)
Lynas (Australia)Supplies the rare earth raw materialAnnounced
LS Cable & SystemReceives the samarium metal for its permanent magnet plantAnnounced

What was announced

  • Investment: KRW 11.6 billion, at LS Eco Energy's existing Vietnam production subsidiary (LSCV) site.
  • Capacity: about 240 tons per year of samarium metal, enough to supply 700–1,000 tons per year of samarium-cobalt (SmCo) permanent magnets.
  • Supply chain structure: Lynas — the only company outside China that separates and commercially produces rare earths — supplies the raw rare earth material; LS Eco Energy processes it into metal in Vietnam; LS Cable & System uses the metal at its permanent magnet factory.
  • Context: this follows an earlier deal in which LS Eco Energy and Lynas each agreed to subscribe to KRW 30 billion of the other's convertible bonds (CBs), a cross-investment that preceded this production tie-up.

Why samarium-cobalt magnets specifically

SmCo permanent magnets retain stable magnetic force at high temperatures better than more common neodymium magnets, which is why they are used mainly in fighter jets, missiles, and other aerospace and defense applications that demand high heat resistance and stability. Samarium metal is the core raw material for that magnet chemistry, which makes a dedicated, non-China samarium supply chain specifically relevant to defense-sector demand rather than to consumer electronics or EV motor magnets, where neodymium dominates.

Why the China angle matters here

Lynas is described in the report as the only company outside China that both separates rare earth elements and produces them commercially at scale, which is the specific reason its partnership with a Korean supplier matters: it is one of the few paths available for building a rare-earth-to-magnet supply chain with no Chinese link at any step. LS Eco Energy CEO Lee Sang-ho is quoted saying that Korea, despite lacking its own rare earth resources, can still become a core link in the global supply chain through high-value-added materials and component manufacturing.

What is not disclosed

  • A start date or timeline for when the Vietnam facility begins production.
  • Pricing or contract terms between LS Eco Energy, Lynas, and LS Cable & System for the metal supply.
  • Which specific defense or aerospace end customers ultimately use LS Cable & System's magnets.

Quick FAQ

What is LS Eco Energy building?
A KRW 11.6 billion samarium metal production facility in Vietnam, with capacity for about 240 tons of samarium metal per year.

Why does this matter for defense supply chains?
Samarium is the key input for samarium-cobalt magnets used in fighter jets and missiles; this facility creates a rare-earth-to-magnet supply chain that avoids China at every step, using Lynas as the raw material source.

Who ends up using the magnets?
LS Cable & System, which operates the permanent magnet plant that will receive the samarium metal produced in Vietnam.
